Tasty Planet: Back for Seconds is a wonderfully absurd, endlessly escalating arcade experience that embraces its premise with full commitment and gleeful chaos. Developed and published by Dingo Games, it expands upon the foundation laid by the original Tasty Planet, refining the core concept while increasing its scale, variety, humor, and replay value. The premise is still brilliantly simple—players control a tiny gray blob designed to clean microscopic bacteria, but due to scientific miscalculation, it consumes everything smaller than itself and grows at a terrifying rate. What begins in a laboratory petri dish quickly becomes a time-traveling feast across eras, continents, and dimensions. The game’s charm lies in its ability to transform a straightforward mechanic into a grand comedic apocalypse, all while maintaining addictive, pick-up-and-play accessibility.

The gameplay revolves around a consistent loop: move the blob around a contained environment, consume objects smaller than you, grow larger, and eventually devour the entire map. What keeps the formula engaging is pacing—each stage introduces new edible hierarchies, object clustering patterns, enemy hazards, movement obstacles, and visual humor. Levels can feel almost puzzle-like as players navigate danger until they reach a size threshold that flips the power dynamic. Early levels focus on crumbs, germs, coins, ants, and utensils, but the game wastes no time scaling upward—soon you’re eating museum exhibits, dinosaurs, castles, oceans, planets, and galaxies. The smooth transition between scales remains one of the game’s greatest strengths, offering a sense of progression that is visually and mechanically satisfying without relying on traditional RPG systems or upgrades.

Control responsiveness enhances the enjoyment. Movement is simple—just directional navigation—but the blob’s momentum, acceleration, and turning radius subtly evolve as it grows, making size more than a visual indicator. Smaller forms allow quick evasion and nimble maneuvering, while gigantic forms feel appropriately weighty and unstoppable. The game also includes different modes, side objectives, bonus levels, and time challenges that encourage replayability, mastery, and optimization. Co-op support adds a layer of chaotic fun, especially when two blobs compete to devour the same environment, turning a casual session into frantic, playful rivalry. These additions refine the original formula and ensure that repetition never feels stale.

Visually, Tasty Planet: Back for Seconds maintains a clean and readable aesthetic that prioritizes clarity over realism. Objects are distinct, color-coded, and recognizable even when swarming the screen, which is crucial given the constant scaling and frantic movement. The hand-drawn, cartoon-style art direction reinforces the game’s playful tone without overwhelming the player with detail. Each historical era—ancient Egypt, feudal Japan, prehistoric landscapes, futuristic cities—receives its own visual flavor and environmental humor. The soundtrack supports this diversity with lighthearted, era-appropriate thematic tracks that enhance atmosphere without distracting from gameplay. Sound effects, particularly the constant chomping, popping, and swallowing noises, contribute heavily to the game’s comedic personality.

Narratively, the game adopts a loose but charming story structure that ties the time-travel premise together through brief illustrated cutscenes. The humor is intentionally simple, family-friendly, and driven by visual exaggeration rather than dialogue-heavy storytelling. It never tries to overshadow gameplay, functioning instead as a whimsical backdrop that contextualizes why a sentient blob keeps jumping across eras consuming everything in sight. The writing lands best when it leans into absurdity, acknowledging the ridiculousness of its world rather than attempting emotional stakes or dramatic weight.

However, like most arcade-style experiences, the game does have limitations. The core mechanic, while addictive, can feel repetitive during long play sessions, especially for players seeking narrative depth, complex systems, or strategic variety. Difficulty spikes occasionally occur when aggressive enemies or environmental hazards overwhelm smaller blobs, leading to moments of frustration. Visually, the environments—though charming—lack the polish or animation depth of larger-budget titles. The simplicity of controls and progression may disappoint those expecting multilayered growth systems, upgrades, or customization. Yet these criticisms largely reflect stylistic intent rather than design flaws—the game is built for quick, satisfying bursts of chaotic fun rather than long-term mechanical complexity.

Ultimately, Tasty Planet: Back for Seconds succeeds because it fully understands the appeal of its premise and executes it with humor, momentum, and accessible design. It offers a playful power fantasy, but one framed through silliness rather than aggression—growing not to dominate enemies, but simply to eat everything in the universe because that’s what the blob does. It’s a celebration of escalation, curiosity, and ridiculous fun. Whether played solo as a relaxing, consumptive romp or shared with friends as a competitive feeding frenzy, the game delivers a consistently entertaining experience. For players who enjoy arcade action, quirky concepts, family-friendly humor, or satisfying progression loops, this sequel remains one of Dingo Games’ most memorable and delightful creations.

The first sequel to a beloved childhood classic, Tasty Planet: Back for Seconds is largely a direct improvement compared to the original in most aspects. Coming back to the game after over 10 years I didn’t find it quite as memorable compared to its predecessor but still had a pretty decent time playing it. 

The game improves upon its predecessor in multiple ways, most notably being the gameplay, introducing the world scaling feature, where upon reaching a certain size the scale of the world increases, making you smaller in comparison as new and larger objects get revealed and the old ones get smaller or outright shrink away. This feature let the developers get much more creative with the level design, and also allowed you to eat a wider variety of things in each level. Before, they had to achieve this by splitting levels up into many slightly different but overall similar individual levels. This also makes the levels a little bit longer than average compared to the previous game. The levels themselves also largely stick to the same ratio of “normal” “themed” and “gimmick” levels as the original, with maybe a few less puzzle themed ones. Finally, the levels all have their own names now instead of just being [area] 1, 2, 3, and so on…

The time requirements for the levels are also slightly more forgiving compared to the first game, although there are still a significant number of levels which still have unreasonable medal times. Unfortunately, the medals have much more significance now, being a requirement in order to unlock various bonus levels.

I don’t think the game originally had any bonus levels when I first played it, or if it did, I certainly can’t remember any of them. Unfortunately, the bonus levels are just as bad here as in the rest of the series, arguably being worse in the fact that over half of them are just the same levels as the story mode but harder. The other bonus levels either are basic levels that probably should have been included in the main story, or more experimental levels that really show how sadistic the developers can get with this game. 

Most bonus levels are locked behind getting a certain amount of gold medals, which considering the games still quite brutal difficulty regarding gold medals makes it more of a chore than anything else. After seeing that most bonus levels were just harder copies of previous levels, I decided it wasn’t worth my time to bother to unlock the last 25% of them. 

Another overall improvement comes with the art quality. The animals in particular got a pretty sizable upgrade in comparison to the first game, and generally most objects (that aren’t just reused from the first game) look quite good and fit their respective area. The far future is probably the exception, where a lot of the stuff there is maybe TOO hammed up with the goofiness but overall, there was a reasonable and respectable improvement over the first game.

They also knocked it out of the park with the music once again, finding 4 more perfect or near perfect tracks to add alongside the original 3. All the tracks really help get you in the zone when it comes to devouring the world.

Despite all the improvements, the game isn’t really as memorable as the first, to the point where I had forgotten an entire section of the game. It’s only a little bit longer, if at all, compared to the first game if you don’t count the “endurance” levels of the first. The overall pacing is also a little strange, going through many ancient periods of history before suddenly jumping straight to the future. The game really could have used either a renaissance or modern time period. 

Once again, they changed the UI from the original version of this game, which I greatly disagree with. The game itself was much less memorable compared to the first so I only found this out after looking at the wiki online, but the overall change is still akin to replacing a metal part with cheap plastic. Fortunately, as far as I could tell it was just the UI that was changed.

Overall, it was still a decent enough experience, especially to relive the nostalgia of the dinosaur levels. It’s a good game on sale, especially if you are a fan of the series and looking to revisit it again, but I wouldn’t say its particularly worth the increased price. My playthrough took 2.7 hours and you can probably expect a similar time yourself.

There are sequels that feel like cash grabs. There are sequels that miss the soul of the original. And then—very rarely—there are sequels like Tasty Planet: Back for Seconds. Games that don’t just follow up on a great experience, but elevate it. This game didn’t just give me more of what I wanted—it gave me everything I didn’t realize I’d been craving.

The original Tasty Planet already had a tight grip on my heart. The chill vibes, the slow escalation, the feeling of starting as a literal speck and ending as a galactic force of nature—that whole formula is so simple and yet so deeply satisfying. But Back for Seconds took all of that, added more polish, more charm, and somehow made it feel even more personal.

The second I launched it, I knew this was going to be a ride. Same idea: you’re still a cute-but-deadly blob, eating everything in your path. But this time, it’s got time travel. TIME. TRAVEL. I’m eating dinosaurs, pharaohs, medieval knights, robots—it’s like every childhood fantasy of chaos packed into one endlessly fun experience. You’re not just growing—you’re growing through history. And I LOVE that.

What makes this game such a massive personal hit for me isn’t just the concept—it’s the fact that it exists at all. Getting a sequel to a game I adored so much as a kid? That’s rare. So many childhood games just faded away, never getting the love or attention they deserved. But this? This feels like a love letter to everyone who played the first one, everyone who grew up watching their favorite YouTubers (I still vividly remember those Let’s Plays!), and everyone who ever smiled at the absurd joy of devouring the entire world, one pixel at a time.

It feels like the devs knew how much this game meant to people like me. Everything is just a bit tighter—the controls feel smoother, the levels are more creative, the pacing is even better. But it’s still true to the original. The charm, the humor, the peaceful background music that slowly morphs into something more dramatic as you grow—it’s all here. But more refined. More confident. More fun.

It’s honestly hard to explain how happy this game makes me. There’s something ridiculously wholesome about it. It doesn’t rely on grindy mechanics, microtransactions, or flashy gimmicks. It’s just you, the blob, the world, and the sweet satisfaction of turning ants into appetizers and cities into crumbs. It’s a dopamine machine in the best way possible.

Even after all this time, I find myself coming back to it. Sometimes I boot it up when I need to relax. Other times I replay a level just to relive the feeling of growing from a grain of sand to a god of consumption. It’s got replayability, but more than that, it has heart. And that’s something a lot of games forget to bring.

I’ll be honest—there’s something really emotional about playing this now. The first game brings back memories. This one creates new ones. It makes me feel like that same wide-eyed kid again, but now I’m in control. I’m not just watching it anymore—I’m playing it, living it, loving it.

So to anyone wondering if the sequel holds up—YES. 1000x yes. It doesn’t just hold up; it surpasses expectations. If you ever loved Tasty Planet, even for a moment, Back for Seconds is absolutely worth your time. It’s not just a game—it’s a celebration of everything that made the original so special, turned up to 11.

Massive shoutout to the developers for bringing this into the world. It’s the kind of game that reminds me why I fell in love with gaming in the first place. No pressure, no stress—just joy, weirdness, and the most fun you can have eating everything in sight.

This sequel? It's a personal masterpiece.
